payload.text: Cities have turned out to be surprisingly good places for bees. Parks, balconies and railway lines offer a longer flowering {{b1}} than the fields around them, where a single crop blooms for a week and then leaves nothing behind. Keeping hives on rooftops has become so {{b2}} in some capitals that experts now warn of the opposite problem: too many colonies competing for the same flowers. The honeybee, after all, is a kind of farm animal, and protecting it does little for the wild species that are genuinely at {{b3}}. What those insects need is not more hives but more {{b4}} ground.

payload.text: Music teachers used to warn that anyone who had not taken up an instrument by the age of ten had left it too {{b1}}. That view has quietly collapsed. Adult beginners learn differently rather than badly: they practise with a clearer {{b2}} of what they want to sound like, and they can tell a teacher exactly which bar is giving them {{b3}}. What they lack is time, and the willingness to sound bad in front of other people. Progress, most teachers now agree, depends far more on how {{b4}} someone practises than on the age at which they begin.

payload.text: Clothes are now made so cheaply that giving them away can cost more than throwing them out. Charity shops in Europe receive far more donations than they can possibly {{b1}}, and much of what arrives is shipped abroad, where a growing share of it is quietly {{b2}} as waste. The industry's own figures suggest that the average garment is worn only a handful of times before it is {{b3}}. Repairing and reselling would help, but both depend on clothes being well made to begin with, and durability is the one {{b4}} that a price tag never shows.

payload.text: Students who type their lecture notes end up with a far more complete {{b1}} than those who write by hand, and remember noticeably less of it. Typing is fast enough to let the words pass straight from the speaker to the screen without being {{b2}} at all. A pen forces a choice about what matters, and that choice is itself a form of {{b3}}. The advice that follows is not to abandon laptops but to slow down: summarise rather than {{b4}}, and read the notes again while the lecture is still fresh.

gaps.before: The findings of the survey bear little
gaps.after: to what the managers had confidently predicted a year earlier.
options: resemblance
similarity

gaps.explanation: bear little / no resemblance to ~（～とほとんど似ていない）は決まった言い方。similarity は have similarities with / there are similarities between の形で使い、bear とは組まない。likeness は「肖像・面影」の意味が中心。comparison は bear comparison with ~（～に匹敵する）となり意味が逆になる。

gaps.before: Not until the final week of the trial
gaps.after: that the drug had been tested on so few patients.
options: did the committee learn
the committee learned
the committee did learn
had the committee learned
gaps.explanation: Not until ~ が文頭に出ると、主節は疑問文と同じ語順（倒置）になるので did the committee learn が正しい。the committee learned は倒置していない。the committee did learn も語順が逆。had the committee learned は倒置の形だが、that 節の had been tested より前の出来事にはならず時制が合わない。

gaps.before: Rain had been falling steadily since dawn.
gaps.after: , the match went ahead exactly as planned.
options: Even so
Because of this
In other words

payload.title: The City That Painted Its Roofs White
paragraphs: Every large city is warmer than the fields around it, and the gap is widest not at noon but around midnight. Brick, concrete and dark asphalt absorb sunlight all afternoon and then release it slowly for hours after dark, so that the air above a dense district can stay four to seven degrees warmer than the air a few kilometres outside. Trees and open soil do the opposite: water evaporating from leaves carries heat away. A neighbourhood built of hard surfaces has almost no way of losing what it has taken in.

The consequence is a night that never cools, and it is the night that does the damage. A body recovers from a hot day only if the temperature drops enough for sleep, and in heatwaves the deaths are concentrated among older residents living on upper floors in the districts with the fewest trees. Air conditioning protects the people who have it while pumping still more heat into the street outside, which is one reason the burden falls so unevenly. The poorest streets are usually the hottest ones, and they were hot long before the current warming began.

What has proved effective is also cheap. Ahmedabad, in western India, began coating the flat roofs of low-income housing with ordinary white lime paint; indoor temperatures fell by two to five degrees for a cost of a few dollars a roof, and the city's heat-warning plan is now copied across South Asia. White surfaces do have limits. They save far more energy in summer than they cost in winter in hot climates, but the balance is closer in northern cities, and paint has to be renewed as it weathers. Planting shade trees does more and lasts longer, though a young tree needs watering for years before it shelters anyone at all.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: Hard urban surfaces keep cities hot at night and the harm falls mainly on the poorest residents, but simple measures such as white roofs and shade trees can bring real relief.
Cities are warmer than the countryside chiefly because so many residents run air conditioning during the hottest hours of the afternoon.
White paint has now solved the problem of urban heat in South Asia, and northern cities should adopt exactly the same policy without changes.
The only lasting answer to urban heat is to plant large numbers of trees, since painted roofs weather too quickly to be of any use.

questions.before: Heatwaves are most dangerous at night because
questions.after: and the strain of the previous day is carried into the next one.
options: the air never cools enough for the body to rest properly
hospitals keep fewer staff on duty after midnight
roofs painted white stop reflecting sunlight once it is dark
older residents tend to leave their windows open while they sleep

questions.prompt: 都市の暑さの負担が住民のあいだで不公平に分かれていることを最もよく示している語句はどれですか。

spans.text: water evaporating from leaves carries heat away
The poorest streets are usually the hottest ones
indoor temperatures fell by two to five degrees

questions.sentence: In other words, the city does not simply get hot; it stores heat and hands it back long after the sun has gone.

questions.prompt: 筆者が本文全体で最も伝えたいことはどれですか。
options: Urban heat is built into the materials cities are made of, so the practical response is to change those surfaces where people actually live, using cheap measures now and slower ones such as trees for the long term.
Because heat affects the poorest districts most, cities should concentrate on supplying air conditioning to every household on an upper floor.
Since a young tree takes years to give shade, planting programmes should be abandoned in favour of painting every roof in the city white.
The temperature difference between a city and the surrounding countryside is too small to justify spending public money on it.

payload.title: The Ferry That Runs on Batteries
paragraphs: The crossing takes twenty minutes, and the ferry has made it more than thirty times a day since 2015 without burning a drop of diesel. Norway's first electric car ferry works because the route is short and utterly predictable: the vessel docks, charges for about ten minutes while the cars roll off and on, and leaves again. The battery it carries is far smaller than the distance would suggest, since it is topped up at both ends rather than filled once a day. The fjord village on one side, however, had a grid too weak to deliver that much power in ten minutes, so a second battery was installed on the quay, charging slowly all day and emptying itself into the ship in short bursts.

The numbers that persuaded other operators were not environmental. Electricity for the route costs a fraction of what the diesel did, and an electric drive has fewer moving parts to service, so the running costs fell by roughly two thirds even though the vessel itself was more expensive to build. What turned a single experiment into a fleet was the way contracts were written: when the transport authority began awarding routes on emissions as well as price, shipyards suddenly had a reason to design for batteries, and dozens of electric ferries followed within a decade.

It would be a mistake to read this as a template for shipping as a whole. A container vessel crossing the Pacific cannot stop to charge, and no battery light enough to carry is large enough to move it; for those routes the argument has moved on to hydrogen and ammonia, neither of which is yet produced cleanly at scale. Ferries were the easy case, and they were solved first for exactly that reason: a ship that returns to the same two quays all day is, in energy terms, barely a ship at all.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: Short, repetitive ferry routes suited batteries so well that electric ferries spread quickly once contracts rewarded low emissions, but the same approach will not work for long-distance shipping.
Electric ferries were adopted across Norway mainly because passengers demanded a quieter and cleaner journey across the fjords.
Battery technology has now advanced far enough for container ships to cross oceans without any fuel at all.
The Norwegian ferry succeeded only because the village grid was strong enough to charge the vessel in ten minutes.

questions.before: A battery was installed on the quay because
questions.after: so the power had to be gathered slowly and released all at once.
options: the local grid could not supply so much electricity in a few minutes
the ship's own battery had begun to fail after ten years of service
the operator wanted to sell surplus electricity back to the village
diesel generators were banned in the fjord by the transport authority

questions.prompt: 一隻の実験が国全体の変化に広がった理由を最もよく示している語句はどれですか。

spans.text: the vessel docks, charges for about ten minutes
an electric drive has fewer moving parts to service
began awarding routes on emissions as well as price
no battery light enough to carry is large enough to move it

questions.sentence: The saving, in short, came from the engine room rather than from any goodwill about the climate.

questions.prompt: 筆者が本文全体で最も伝えたいことはどれですか。
options: Electrification works where a route is short and repeated, and it spread because it was cheaper to run and because the rules rewarded it; the harder half of shipping still has no answer.
Because ocean shipping cannot use batteries, the money spent on electric ferries in Norway should have been saved for hydrogen research.
Any vessel can be converted to batteries provided a second battery is installed on the quay to make up for a weak local grid.
The main lesson of the Norwegian ferry is that transport authorities should award every contract to the cheapest bidder available.
